extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, law students, inventors, and anyone drafting or litigating patent claims
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for how patent claims are drafted, structured, categorized, and interpreted in prosecution and litigation (including U.S. case-law hooks and statutory references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims define extent of protection
rubrics_metrics.description: In a patent or patent application, the claims define, in technical terms, the extent of the protection conferred by a patent or the protection sought in a patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are sentences that define the invention and play the central role in patent litigation: they are the metes and bounds of the patentee's exclusive right. Draft claims carefully because they determine infringement and validity disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim structure (preamble, transitional phrase, body)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is generally a single sentence with three parts: preamble, transitional phrase, and body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preamble: introduces the type of subject matter being claimed (e.g., 'A method of,' 'A system for'). Transitional phrase: connects preamble to body; examples include 'comprising' (open), 'consisting of' (closed), and 'consisting essentially of' (semi-closed). Body: the list of elements/limitations of the invention. Use the proper transitional phrase to control open vs closed scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent vs dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent claim: stands alone and defines the broadest scope sought. Dependent claim: references an earlier claim and adds further limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent claims inherit all limitations of their parent and are organized in a hierarchy. A typical patent has 1–4 independent claims and many dependent claims. Use dependent claims to add fallback positions and narrower claim scopes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product (apparatus/machine/composition) claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Product claims (also called apparatus, machine, composition of matter, manufacture) cover physical things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use product claims to protect tangible inventions and structural features. Draft element-by-element in the body to delineate the physical components or composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method / process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Method or process claims cover a series of steps or actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft clear step language and the order/relationship between steps if order is material. Consider infringement patterns (performing steps) and potential for divided infringement issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use claims (second medical use / EPO-style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use claims cover the use of a known thing for a new purpose; these are more common in the EPO than the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different jurisdictions treat ‘use’ claims differently; consider filing formats (e.g., purpose-limited product claims, Swiss-type historically) appropriate to the target office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function claims (U.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Means-plus-function claims recite a function performed by undisclosed structure and are construed under 35 U.S.C. §112(f) (or pre-AIA §112 paragraph 6) as covering the corresponding structure in the specification and equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If invoking means-plus-function style, ensure the specification discloses adequate structure corresponding to the claimed function; otherwise the claim may be limited or indefinite. Be aware of how courts limit scope to disclosed structure and equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauregard claims (computer-readable medium claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauregard claims (U.S.) recite a computer-readable medium storing instructions (used in software-related patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These claims attempt to claim software by reciting a medium with program instructions. Jurisdictional case law and patentability rules for software should be considered when using this claim form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush claims (chemistry combinatorial claiming)
rubrics_metrics.description: Markush claims, used in chemistry, recite a closed group of alternatives (e.g., a list of substituents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Markush format to claim a group of chemical alternatives; ensure the alternatives form a patentably relevant and supported group under the specification and practice-specific rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jepson claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Jepson claims recite known elements in the preamble and the improvement in the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jepson claims can admit the preamble subject matter as prior art, which may be undesirable in U.S. practice. They are rare in the U.S. for that reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Swiss-type claims (historical second medical use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Swiss-type claims were used (formerly at the EPO) for second medical use claims and are generally disused now.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize historical claim formats may be obsolete or replaced by newer claim drafting approaches in particular jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard (U.S.: Phillips v. AWH)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are interpreted by courts during litigation; in the U.S., claim terms get their ordinary meaning to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention, in light of the specification and prosecution history (Phillips v. AWH, Fed. Cir. 2005, en banc).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting, use specification language to shape how a POSITA will understand claim terms, and be mindful of prosecution history statements that can later affect construction. Consider prosecution and specification language to support desired interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim can be infringed not only literally but also under the doctrine of equivalents: an accused product that performs substantially the same function in substantially the same way to achieve substantially the same result (Graver Tank).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The doctrine is limited by prosecution history estoppel and the all-elements rule. Evaluate claim scope for both literal infringement and equivalents; prosecution disclaimers may narrow application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim indefiniteness (35 U.S.C. §112(b) and Nautilus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. §112(b), a claim must 'particularly point out and distinctly claim' the invention. Nautilus v. Biosig (2014) established that a claim is indefinite if its scope is not reasonably certain to a person of ordinary skill in the art in light of the specification and prosecution history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims with clear boundaries and supported definitions; vague or ambiguous terms risk invalidation for indefiniteness under the reasonably-certain standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim differentiation doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: A doctrine that presumes different claims have different scope: a limitation in a dependent claim is presumed not to limit the independent claim from which it depends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use claim differentiation as an interpretive aid in litigation, but it's a presumption, not an absolute rule. Draft dependent claims thoughtfully to preserve interpretive flexibility.
